**What the story is about, in plain terms**

ForgeMark is a load-testing tool. It fires thousands of fake "agents" at a git server at the same time, each one pushing commits, and measures how fast the server keeps up. Think of it as a stress test for GitHub-style services.

While the test runs, every agent reports its result to one shared object called the collector. The collector counts operations and keeps timings so the dashboard can draw live charts. Because many agents write to it at once, it is protected by a lock. Only one agent can update it at a time.

Any engineer looking at that code has the same instinct: "thousands of agents, one lock, that must be a bottleneck. Let's split it into many smaller locks." That is called sharding the mutex. It is a classic optimisation and it sounds obviously right.

Someone on the team already had that idea, looked into it, and rejected it. The reason is in the recorded fact: the lock only guards a counter increment and an append, which take nanoseconds. The git operations around it take tens to hundreds of milliseconds. The lock is held for a vanishingly small fraction of the time, so splitting it gains nothing. The fact also says when to reopen the question: only if profiling shows real contention.

That is the demo beat. In step 2 you ask the brain for help with "make the collector lock faster", as if you were about to start the work. It gives you the right files, but it also hands you the prior decision before you write a line. In step 3 you ask directly and get the full rationale plus the condition for revisiting. Nobody had to remember this. It was not in a doc. It came out of a past coding session and was distilled into a durable fact.

Three separate questions, three different answers.

**Who decides promotion: a human, always.** Nothing moves a fact from one branch to another automatically. A git merge of the code does not merge the facts. Someone runs `entire brain facts promote --from <branch> --into main` on purpose, and picks a conflict strategy if both sides have a fact on the same topic. That is why the four merged feature branches in this repo still hold 31 facts that main does not have. Nobody has promoted them.

**Is it working behind the scenes: yes, on a schedule.** Setup installed one machine-wide watcher, a launchd service on your Mac. Every five minutes it checks each registered repo and refreshes the cheap, deterministic parts: the code index, the session list, docs, history. When new sessions have ended, it also runs distillation at a bounded cadence. So the 23 of 23 sessions distilled you see in status happened without you running anything. content.text:
**What the demo target is.** ForgeMark's web GUI accepts a special remote of the form `demo://`. Instead of pushing to a real forge, it synthesises push results locally: each fake agent sleeps for a sampled latency, then reports success or failure. The whole pipeline downstream of that, the collector, the live charts, the race view, result persistence, runs exactly as it would against a real forge. It exists so you can exercise and demo the tool with no network and no credentials.

**What the parameters mean.** They are query parameters on the URL, defined in the demo runner:

| parameter | meaning | default |
|---|---|---|
| p50 | median latency per push | 80ms |
| spread | how heavy the tail is, roughly p99 divided by p50 | 3 |
| err | probability a push fails | 0.01 |
| cas | probability a push is a compare-and-swap rejection | 0 |
| cap | ops per second ceiling, latency inflates as you approach it, like a real forge queueing | unbounded |

So `demo://fast?p50=60ms&err=0.01` means a forge whose typical push takes 60 milliseconds, with one push in a hundred failing. The README's own example adds `spread=3&cap=400`.

**Why it makes a good fact.** The code and README say what the parameters do. They do not say which profile the team uses for recordings or why. That decision exists only in whoever's head set it up. If you tell Claude Code "demo recordings use demo://fast with p50=60ms and err=0.01 because a real forge makes race timing non-reproducible on camera", you are writing down a convention, with its reason, that no grep could find. When Codex then answers "use demo://fast with p50=60ms and err=0.01", the only possible source is the brain. That is the point of the segment: the why crossed from one vendor's agent to another through the repo.

**The reason clause is doing real work.** Against a live forge, two takes of the same race give different numbers, because the forge's load varies. On camera you want the same curve every take. The synthetic target gives you that. The clause also makes the fact a decision rather than a bare setting, which is the kind the brain is for. Make sure it is true for you. If your team actually records against a real Entire target, change the fact to match. The brain should not learn something false on video.

**Why recall finds it.** The question "I'm recording a ForgeMark demo. Which target and latency profile should I use, and why?" shares "demo", "recording" and "target" with the fact, and the embedding rerank will pick up "latency profile" against "p50". I verified earlier that a question with no matching fact returns an unrelated top hit, so the shared vocabulary is what makes this land in first place. Run the Codex question once before filming and confirm the fact comes back under its ID.

**The path to give it.** Pass `--path workflow.docs.convention` or let the agent classify it. Classification will land it as a convention under workflow, which is right.

# commits at every forge simultaneously for one minute, rendered as a live
# head-to-head race (the GUI's #race view — big counters, lanes, a podium).

Good choice, and the code confirms the shape. The script and the GUI preset both set 16 agents and 60 seconds, with warm-up at zero so the race counts from the gun, and commits of 1 to 3 files of 1KB each, which the script itself calls checkpoint-sized. All of that is the "what", and it is in the README, so Codex could grep it.

The "why" is not written anywhere. The only hint in the repo is a comment warning that raising concurrency is risky on a public forge. The reason I drafted, that 16 for 60 seconds matches a typical checkpoint burst from an agent fleet and that longer runs hit replica rebalancing, was a plausible shape, not something I found. You need to replace it with the real reason, since this goes on video and into the brain.

**The fact, with the reason left for you to fill**

In Claude Code:

```
Remember that the push race preset is 16 agents for 60 seconds because <your real reason>.
```

Candidates for the reason, pick whichever is true:

- 16 concurrent pushes of 1 to 3 small files is what a fleet of coding agents checkpointing looks like, so the race measures the real workload, not a synthetic one.
- 60 seconds is long enough for throughput to settle on both forges and short enough to hold an audience in a live demo.
- Above 16, a public forge's abuse limiter can trip mid-race and wreck the comparison.

If more than one is true, say both. A fact with two reasons is fine.

**The Codex question**

```
Why does the ForgeMark push race preset use 16 agents for 60 seconds?
```

It shares "push race preset", "16 agents" and "60 seconds" with the fact, so recall ranks it first. Codex may also find the README and the script, which is fine: it will show the setting from the code and the reason from the brain, and you narrate the difference. "The code says what. The brain says why. Only one of those survives a session ending."

**On camera, the beat**

1. In Claude Code, type the remember line. It reports a fact ID. Say: "Claude Code just learned why. I close it."
2. Open Codex in the same repo, same branch. Type the question.
3. Codex runs recall, quotes the fact Claude Code wrote a minute ago, with its ID, and gives the reason. Say: "Different agent, different vendor, same memory. The why lives in the repo, not in the tool."

Run step 2 and 3 once before filming so you have seen it land.

Say: "Let's demo Brain, which together with entire-graph, that we saw in another video, gives your repository Continuous Memory. What's on screen is a repo's brain. In a minute I'll show you how to get this up for your own repo. First, what it does for you.

Every day developers and agents make decisions, hit constraints, and learn what works. Most of that vanishes when the session ends. The next task starts with the code, but without the experience that produced it. Brain keeps that experience in the repo, not in any one agent. Claude Code, Codex, any agent Entire supports, reads from the same memory.

What that gets you: no task starts from zero. The agent already knows where the code is, which sessions touched it, and what the team learned doing it.

The memory is kept as durable facts, and every fact has a kind. Closed-negative: we tried it and said no, and here is the reason and what would reopen it. This is the one that stops an agent redoing a rejected experiment. Decision: what we chose and why. Gotcha: a trap someone already fell into, so the next one doesn't. Invariant: a rule that must always hold, whoever is editing. Convention and preference: how the team works and what it likes.

Every fact points back to the session it came from. Here is how it works. Graph gives the agent a map of the code. When an agent session ends, a cheap model reads the transcript once and distills what was decided and why. A watcher keeps all of it matching the code. After that it is plain search, fast enough to run at the top of every task.


Say: "The decision on its own, with the condition to reopen it: profiling shows contention. Otherwise leave it. The lines below are the search showing its work. Two of them are invariants explaining why anyone cared: the collector sits on the measured path, so anything slow in there distorts the benchmark itself."

**Claude Code**

Say: "I did that by hand so you could see it. Here is what it looks like when nobody is watching."

Type:
```
Make the collector lock faster. Thousands of agents write to it concurrently. Before you touch any code, run the brain brief and recall for prior decisions about this lock, and tell me what you find before proposing any change.
```

Say: "No grep. Graph finds the code, Brain finds the decision. It didn't start the work. It told me why not to, and what evidence would change that. Now let's teach it something."

Type:
```
Run exactly this command and tell me the fact id it returns: entire brain remember "The push race preset is 16 agents for 60 seconds because above 16 a public forge's abuse limiter can trip mid-race and wreck the comparison" --path workflow.benchmark.rules --json
```

Say: "Claude Code just learned why the race preset is what it is. That reason is written nowhere in the code. I close Claude Code."

**Codex**

Say: "Same repo, same branch, different vendor."

Type:
```
Check the repository brain with entire brain recall, then answer: why does the ForgeMark push race preset use 16 agents for 60 seconds? Quote the fact you found and its id.
```

Say: "The code says what. The brain says why. Codex just read a fact that Claude Code wrote a minute ago. Different agent, different vendor, same memory."

**Closing**

Say: "That is Continuous Memory. An agent works, the session ends, a model distills what was decided, and the next agent inherits it. The July session that produced that collector-lock fact was an agent session. The fact was written by a model. Today another agent read it. No human touched it at any point.

The brain stopped an agent from redoing an optimisation the team already tested and rejected months ago, and told it exactly what evidence would make it worth trying again. Then one agent taught it something, and a different agent learned it. The why lives in the repo, next to the code."
